stem: A business intelligence team needs to build interactive dashboards on top of data stored in Amazon S3 in Parquet format. Queries must run ad-hoc and the team does not want to manage any servers or ETL pipelines. Which combination of AWS services enables this with the least operational overhead?

answers.A: Load the Parquet files into Amazon Redshift and use Redshift to power Amazon QuickSight dashboards.
answers.B: Register the S3 data as a table in AWS Glue Data Catalog, query it with Amazon Athena, and visualize results in Amazon QuickSight connected to Athena.
answers.C: Set up an Amazon EMR cluster, run Spark SQL queries on the Parquet files, and export results to QuickSight.
answers.D: Copy the Parquet files into Amazon RDS Aurora and connect QuickSight directly to Aurora.

explanation: Athena is a serverless query engine that queries S3 data directly using the Glue Data Catalog for schema. QuickSight connects natively to Athena as a data source, completing a fully serverless BI stack with no ETL or server management. Redshift, EMR, and RDS all require provisioning and data loading steps.
tags: Data transfer services with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS DataSync, AWS Storage Gateway)
Data transformation services with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS Glue)

stem: A data analytics team has streaming clickstream data flowing into Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose, which delivers it to Amazon S3. They need to visualize trends in near-real time (within 1 minute) on a dashboard. Which approach meets the near-real-time requirement with the least infrastructure to manage?

answers.A: Configure Kinesis Data Firehose to deliver to Amazon Redshift and connect Amazon QuickSight to Redshift.
answers.B: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics (SQL) to query the stream, write results to DynamoDB, and build a custom dashboard that polls DynamoDB.
answers.C: Deliver the stream to Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon ES) via Kinesis Data Firehose and use OpenSearch Dashboards (Kibana) to visualize near-real-time data.
answers.D: Write a Lambda function that reads from the Kinesis stream every 60 seconds, stores aggregates in S3, and triggers an Athena query that feeds QuickSight SPICE.

explanation: OpenSearch Service (with Dashboards) is designed for near-real-time log and event visualization and integrates natively with Kinesis Data Firehose. Redshift and Athena/SPICE refresh cycles are minutes-to-hours, not sub-minute. A custom DynamoDB + dashboard solution adds significant development and operational work.
tags: Data analytics and visualization services with appropriate use cases (for example, Amazon Athena, AWS Lake Formation, Amazon QuickSuite)

stem: A company needs to migrate a Windows-based HPC workload to AWS. The workload requires a shared file system with SMB protocol support, Active Directory integration, and sub-millisecond latency. The solution must be fully managed. Which AWS storage service is most appropriate?

answers.A: Amazon EFS in Max I/O mode.
answers.B: Amazon S3 with AWS Transfer Family using an SFTP endpoint.
answers.C: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server.
answers.D: Amazon FSx for Lustre.

explanation: FSx for Windows File Server is a fully managed SMB-based file system with native Active Directory integration, designed for Windows workloads. EFS uses NFS (not SMB). S3 with Transfer Family is for file transfer, not a shared file system. FSx for Lustre is a high-performance POSIX file system for Linux HPC workloads.
tags: AWS storage services with appropriate use cases (for example, Amazon FSx, Amazon EFS, Amazon S3, Amazon EBS)
Selecting the most cost-effective storage service for a workload

stem: A stateless REST API runs on an EC2 Auto Scaling group. During peak hours, CPU utilization reaches 90% on all instances and response times increase. The architect must decide between scaling horizontally (adding more instances) or vertically (upgrading to a larger instance type). Which approach is more appropriate for a stateless application and why?

answers.A: Horizontal scaling: add more instances of the same type. Stateless applications share no session state between instances, so requests can be load-balanced across any instance, and scaling out is faster and more resilient.
answers.B: Vertical scaling: upgrade to a larger instance. This reduces the number of instances to manage and eliminates the need for a load balancer.
answers.C: Vertical scaling: a single large instance has lower networking overhead than multiple small instances communicating with a load balancer.
answers.D: Horizontal scaling: add more instances, but only works if the application uses sticky sessions to pin users to a specific instance.

explanation: Stateless applications are ideally suited for horizontal scaling: any instance can handle any request, Auto Scaling can add or remove instances dynamically, and the architecture tolerates individual instance failures. Vertical scaling has upper limits (maximum instance size) and introduces a single point of failure. Sticky sessions are needed for stateful, not stateless, applications.
tags: Scaling strategies (for example, auto scaling, hibernation)
Selecting the appropriate instance family for a workload

stem: A company runs both a production e-commerce platform and a development/testing environment on AWS. The production environment must have 99.99% availability. The development environment is used only on weekdays and can tolerate interruptions. Which combination of EC2 purchasing options optimizes cost for both environments?

answers.A: Use On-Demand Instances for both production and development to ensure maximum reliability.
answers.B: Use Reserved Instances (1-year, no-upfront) for production and Spot Instances for the development environment.
answers.C: Use Spot Instances for both production and development to minimize costs.
answers.D: Use On-Demand for production and Reserved Instances for development.

explanation: Reserved Instances provide capacity guarantees and significant cost savings (up to 40%) for steady-state production workloads. Spot Instances offer up to 90% savings and are appropriate for interruptible development/testing workloads. Using Spot for production risks unexpected interruptions. Using On-Demand for dev/test wastes budget.
tags: AWS purchasing options (for example, Spot Instances, Reserved Instances, Savings Plans)

stem: A company must transfer 500 TB of historical data from on-premises to Amazon S3 within 2 weeks. Their internet connection is 1 Gbps and is fully utilized by production workloads. What is the most practical transfer solution?

answers.A: Use AWS DataSync over the existing internet connection to transfer data in the background.
answers.B: Upgrade the internet connection to 10 Gbps and use aws s3 sync for the transfer.
answers.C: Order multiple AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices to physically transport the data to AWS.
answers.D: Use Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration to speed up uploads over the existing connection.

explanation: Transferring 500 TB over a 1 Gbps link (even at full utilization) would take over 45 days. Snowball Edge devices each hold up to 80 TB; 7 devices would move 500 TB physically within days. DataSync and aws s3 sync are limited by internet bandwidth. Upgrading connectivity takes longer than 2 weeks to provision. Transfer Acceleration improves upload performance but is still constrained by the 1 Gbps pipe.
tags: Data transfer services with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS DataSync, AWS Storage Gateway)

stem: A company wants to run containerized microservices on AWS. The team is familiar with Kubernetes and wants to use standard Kubernetes APIs and tooling (kubectl, Helm, etc.) while minimizing cluster management overhead. Which service is most appropriate?

answers.A: Amazon ECS on EC2 with a custom task definition that supports kubectl commands.
answers.B: Amazon EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service), which runs managed Kubernetes control plane and supports standard Kubernetes APIs, kubectl, and Helm.
answers.C: AWS Fargate without an orchestrator, running containers directly on serverless compute.
answers.D: AWS Elastic Beanstalk, which supports Docker containers with automatic orchestration.

explanation: EKS is AWS's managed Kubernetes service that runs a compliant Kubernetes control plane and supports all standard Kubernetes tooling. Teams already familiar with Kubernetes can use EKS with no tooling changes. ECS uses AWS-specific task definitions and does not support kubectl. Fargate is a compute engine used with ECS or EKS, not a standalone orchestrator. Elastic Beanstalk is not a Kubernetes-compatible service.
tags: AWS compute services with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS Batch, Amazon EMR, AWS Fargate)
Selecting the appropriate compute options and features (for example, EC2 instance types) to meet business requirements

stem: A company runs a MySQL 5.7 database on EC2. They want to migrate to a managed service without changing the MySQL engine. Which migration is homogeneous and which tool migrates the data with minimal downtime?

answers.A: Migrate to Amazon RDS for MySQL or Amazon Aurora MySQL (homogeneous migration). Use AWS DMS with Full Load + CDC to replicate data continuously until cutover.
answers.B: Migrate to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL (heterogeneous migration). Use AWS SCT to convert the schema and DMS to migrate data.
answers.C: Migrate to Amazon Redshift (heterogeneous migration). Use AWS Glue to transform and load MySQL data.
answers.D: Migrate to Amazon DynamoDB (heterogeneous migration). Use AWS Database Migration Service in NoSQL migration mode.

explanation: MySQL to RDS/Aurora MySQL is a homogeneous migration — same engine family, no schema conversion required. DMS with Full Load + CDC provides near-zero-downtime migration. Aurora PostgreSQL and DynamoDB are heterogeneous targets requiring additional conversion. Redshift is an analytical data warehouse, not a drop-in MySQL replacement.
tags: Determining an appropriate database engine (for example, MySQL compared with PostgreSQL)

stem: A company is building a data lake in Amazon S3. Raw data from various sources lands in S3 and must be catalogued automatically so analysts can discover and query it with Amazon Athena. Which AWS service should be used to crawl the S3 data and populate a metadata catalog?

answers.A: AWS Glue Crawlers, which automatically scan S3 data, infer schemas, and create/update tables in the AWS Glue Data Catalog.
answers.B: Amazon Macie, which classifies S3 data and creates a data inventory.
answers.C: Amazon Athena, which can directly infer schemas from S3 files without a catalog.
answers.D: AWS Lake Formation Blueprint, which automatically imports data from databases into S3 and creates catalog entries.

explanation: Glue Crawlers scan S3 paths, detect file formats and schemas, and populate the Glue Data Catalog with table definitions that Athena uses for queries. Macie is a security service for sensitive data detection. Athena requires pre-defined table definitions (via Glue Data Catalog or manual DDL). Lake Formation Blueprints import data from databases into S3 but don't crawl existing S3 data.
tags: Transforming data between formats (for example, .csv to .parquet)

stem: A media company runs a workflow that ingests uploaded videos, triggers parallel transcode and metadata extraction steps, retries failed steps with exponential backoff, and sends a final callback only after all branches succeed. The workload volume fluctuates heavily, and the team wants minimal infrastructure management. Which design BEST fits the requirement?

answers.A: Use Amazon ECS services for each stage with EventBridge rules and custom state-tracking tables in DynamoDB.
answers.B: Use AWS Batch for all steps and poll job states from an AWS Lambda coordinator.
answers.C: Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate parallel branches and retries, with AWS Lambda and service integrations for each task.
answers.D: Use Amazon MQ with worker consumers and implement workflow state transitions in application code.

explanation: The requirement is orchestration-centric: parallel branches, retries, backoff, and completion coordination with minimal ops. Step Functions is purpose-built for this serverless pattern and reduces custom state-management code. Other options can implement the behavior but require significant custom orchestration logic and operational overhead.

stem: A company is modernizing a monolithic Java application that requires sidecar agents for service mesh, custom kernel tuning, and strict control over container runtime behavior. Teams already run Kubernetes on-prem and need workload portability between on-prem and AWS with minimal re-platforming risk. Which compute strategy is MOST suitable?

answers.A: Refactor into AWS Lambda functions and use API Gateway for all service endpoints.
answers.B: Adopt Amazon EKS and deploy the existing Kubernetes manifests with incremental adjustments.
answers.C: Use Amazon ECS on Fargate because it removes all cluster management and supports all Kubernetes-native controls.
answers.D: Migrate directly to AWS App Runner to preserve all current sidecar and runtime controls.

explanation: The key signal is Kubernetes portability plus deep runtime control requirements. EKS aligns best with existing K8s operations and minimizes migration risk from on-prem Kubernetes. Lambda is a major re-architecture; Fargate/ECS simplifies operations but does not provide Kubernetes-native portability and control parity; App Runner is not designed for this level of runtime customization.

stem: A high-throughput TCP gaming backend must expose static anycast IPs globally and handle millions of long-lived connections. The team is evaluating ALB, NLB, and GWLB, and wants the most cost-efficient service that still meets protocol and latency requirements. Which choice is MOST appropriate?

answers.A: Use ALB because L7 routing is cheaper for all connection types and supports static IPs natively.
answers.B: Use NLB because it supports L4 TCP at high scale with static IP/EIP support and lower overhead for this traffic profile.
answers.C: Use GWLB because it is optimized for distributing internet-facing application traffic directly to containers.
answers.D: Use ALB plus Global Accelerator because ALB is required for all long-lived TCP sessions.

explanation: For massive TCP workloads needing static IP semantics, NLB is the right fit and is typically more cost-effective than ALB for pure L4 forwarding at scale. ALB is L7 and does not natively provide the same static IP model. GWLB is for transparent appliance insertion, not general application load balancing.

stem: A workload runs continuously at 20-30% CPU on c6i.4xlarge instances, with memory utilization under 40%. Performance tests show c6i.2xlarge meets latency SLOs with 55% CPU at peak. Which action provides the BEST cost optimization with controlled risk?

answers.A: Keep the current size and purchase a 3-year Compute Savings Plan immediately.
answers.B: Switch to t3 instances because burst credits always lower cost for steady workloads.
answers.C: Move to Spot Instances only because interruption risk is negligible for all production traffic.
answers.D: Right-size to c6i.2xlarge in a phased rollout with CloudWatch alarms and rollback thresholds.

explanation: The data indicates systematic over-provisioning, and validated load tests show smaller instances still meet SLOs. Right-sizing with phased deployment and rollback controls is the best cost/risk tradeoff. Savings Plans optimize pricing but do not solve over-sizing. T-class and Spot-only choices introduce different performance/availability risks for a steady production profile.

stem: A team ingests sensitive clickstream data to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams from private subnets. They must avoid internet egress, enforce least-privilege producer permissions, and encrypt records with customer-managed keys. Which design is MOST secure and operationally efficient?

answers.A: Route producer traffic through a NAT gateway to the public Kinesis endpoint and use SSE-S3 encryption.
answers.B: Use an internet gateway, allow egress only to AWS IP ranges, and rely on default Kinesis encryption.
answers.C: Use VPC peering to a shared services VPC and publish with wildcard IAM permissions on all streams.
answers.D: Use an interface VPC endpoint (PrivateLink) for Kinesis, grant producers IAM permissions scoped to specific stream ARNs, and enable KMS CMK encryption on the stream.

explanation: PrivateLink removes internet egress dependency for Kinesis access from private subnets. Stream-level IAM scoping enforces least privilege, and CMK-backed encryption meets strict key-control requirements. NAT/internet-based options increase exposure and operational/cost overhead.
tags: Secure access to ingestion access points

stem: A company must migrate 120 TB of archived compliance files to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval at the lowest total cost. Most files are on-prem and disconnected from applications; no incremental sync is needed after migration. The site has only a 200 Mbps link and a 3-week deadline. Which option is MOST cost-effective and feasible?

answers.A: Use AWS DataSync continuously over the 200 Mbps link until all files are uploaded.
answers.B: Use AWS Snowball Edge for bulk transfer, then lifecycle objects to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.
answers.C: Use AWS Transfer Family SFTP endpoints and ask teams to upload archives manually.
answers.D: Use S3 Transfer Acceleration from on-prem clients with multipart uploads.

explanation: The constrained bandwidth and deadline make network transfer impractical. Snowball Edge is designed for large offline bulk migration and minimizes transfer time risk. DataSync and Transfer Acceleration are network dependent; Transfer Family is not suited for this bulk archival migration model.
tags: Selecting the most cost-effective storage service for a workload

stem: A company is migrating from Oracle on-premises to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. Management wants to minimize migration licensing and transformation cost while reducing cutover risk. Which DMS strategy is MOST cost-effective and appropriate?

answers.A: Use homogeneous migration tooling because both engines are relational and require no conversion.
answers.B: Use AWS DMS with AWS SCT for heterogeneous schema conversion and ongoing CDC until cutover.
answers.C: Export Oracle tables to CSV and bulk load manually into Aurora to avoid DMS costs.
answers.D: Replicate Oracle block storage with AWS DataSync and attach it directly to Aurora.

explanation: Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL is a heterogeneous migration, so schema and code conversion is needed. AWS SCT + DMS (with CDC) is typically the most controlled and cost-effective AWS-native path for minimizing downtime and migration risk. Homogeneous assumptions are incorrect, and manual CSV pipelines increase operational risk and transformation effort.
tags: AWS cost management tools with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, AWS Cost and Usage Report)

stem: An API platform is seeing runaway downstream cost due to abusive client traffic. The team needs a throttling strategy that protects backend systems and reduces excess spend without blocking normal burst behavior from legitimate customers. Which design is BEST?

answers.A: Apply a single global fixed rate limit in security groups to all clients equally.
answers.B: Disable API caching and rely on larger backend instances to absorb spikes.
answers.C: Use only AWS Budgets alerts and notify operators after overspend is detected.
answers.D: Use API Gateway usage plans and per-client throttles/quotas, combined with AWS WAF rate-based rules for abusive patterns.

explanation: Cost control and protection require proactive traffic governance. API Gateway usage plans provide tenant-aware throttling and quotas, while WAF rate-based rules mitigate abusive behavior patterns. Budgets are reactive, and infrastructure overprovisioning without traffic controls raises cost.

stem: A company runs a mix of workloads on EC2: a 24/7 production web tier (steady 40 instances), a batch processing tier that bursts to 200 instances for 6-hour windows 3 days a week, and a dev/test tier that is unpredictable but rarely exceeds 20 instances at any time. Finance wants to reduce compute spend by at least 40% without impacting availability. Which combination of purchasing options best achieves this?

answers.A: Purchase 40 Standard Reserved Instances (1-year, all-upfront) for web, 200 Scheduled Reserved Instances for batch, and On-Demand for dev/test.
answers.B: Purchase a Compute Savings Plan covering 40 instances for web and 200 instances for batch combined; use On-Demand for overflow and dev/test.
answers.C: Purchase a Compute Savings Plan sized to cover the 40 steady-state web instances plus typical batch baseline; use Spot Instances with diversified instance pools for batch bursting; use On-Demand or Spot for dev/test.
answers.D: Purchase 240 Standard Reserved Instances (3-year, no-upfront) to cover peak capacity for all tiers and use On-Demand when reservations are exhausted.

explanation: Compute Savings Plans provide the broadest flexibility across instance families and regions and should cover the predictable baseline. Spot Instances are ideal for fault-tolerant batch bursting and deliver up to 90% savings. Dev/test is unpredictable, so On-Demand or Spot avoids waste. Buying reservations for peak batch capacity wastes money during the 18 hours/week it isn't running, and Scheduled RIs are no longer available for new purchases.

stem: An enterprise operates 80 AWS accounts under AWS Organizations. The security team mandates that all S3 buckets must have server-side encryption enabled and public access blocked, all EC2 instances must belong to approved AMIs, and all non-compliant resources must trigger automated remediation within 15 minutes. They want centralized visibility and minimal per-account configuration. What is the MOST operationally efficient approach?

answers.A: Deploy individual AWS Config rules in each account using CloudFormation StackSets, aggregate findings in a central S3 bucket via a Lambda function, and configure SNS notifications for non-compliance.
answers.B: Enable AWS Config with a delegated administrator account, deploy an Organization-level Conformance Pack containing the required managed rules and automatic remediation SSM Automation documents, and use the Config Aggregator to view compliance centrally.
answers.C: Use AWS Security Hub with CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark across all accounts, configure EventBridge rules to trigger Lambda for remediation, and store findings in a central Security Hub master account.
answers.D: Write custom AWS Lambda functions in each account to evaluate resource configuration on a schedule, publish results to Amazon CloudWatch, and use CloudWatch Alarms for out-of-compliance notifications.

explanation: Organization-level Conformance Packs deploy managed Config rules and remediation actions to all accounts simultaneously from a delegated administrator, providing centralized governance with minimal per-account work. Config Aggregators provide cross-account visibility. Security Hub provides findings but doesn't natively enforce Config-rule-based remediation at org level; individual rule deployment via StackSets requires more per-account management.
tags: Access controls and management across multiple accounts
AWS security best practices (for example, the principle of least privilege)

stem: A cloud governance team needs to enforce a baseline infrastructure configuration (VPC with required subnets, an IAM role for SSM access, and CloudTrail enabled) across all new AWS accounts provisioned through AWS Control Tower's Account Factory. New accounts are expected at a rate of 10 per month and must be compliant within minutes of creation. Which approach meets these requirements with the least operational overhead?

answers.A: Create a CloudFormation StackSet targeting all accounts in the organization. Configure it to auto-deploy on new account creation using SERVICE_MANAGED permissions. Trigger a StackSet operation via EventBridge when an Organizations CreateAccount event fires.
answers.B: Build a Lambda function that the Control Tower lifecycle event triggers. The Lambda assumes a cross-account role in the new account and calls CloudFormation to create a stack from a template stored in S3.
answers.C: Use AWS Service Catalog to publish the baseline infrastructure products, share the portfolio with all accounts, and instruct account owners to launch the products upon receiving their account credentials.
answers.D: Use Account Factory for Terraform (AFT) or Control Tower Account Factory customizations (CfCT) to include a CloudFormation template that deploys the baseline resources as part of the account vending pipeline.

explanation: Control Tower's Account Factory Customizations (CfCT) or AFT integrates directly with the account provisioning workflow, applying templates automatically before the account is handed to the owner. This is the purpose-built mechanism for zero-touch baseline enforcement. EventBridge + Lambda is viable but adds operational complexity. Service Catalog requires manual action by account owners, violating the automation requirement.
tags: Design secure access to AWS resources

stem: A company is decomposing a monolith into microservices on Amazon ECS. One downstream payment service is intermittently slow (p99 latency spikes to 30 seconds), causing upstream services to exhaust their thread pools and cascade-fail across the entire system. The team wants to implement a circuit-breaker pattern with automatic recovery, without modifying application code. Which solution achieves this?

answers.A: Deploy AWS App Mesh with an Envoy sidecar proxy for each ECS task. Configure an Envoy circuit-breaker policy with outlier detection (consecutive 5xx errors) and a retry policy with exponential backoff on the virtual service for the payment service.
answers.B: Place an Application Load Balancer in front of the payment service and configure ALB target group health checks with a threshold of 2 consecutive failures; unhealthy targets are removed and the upstream receives 502 errors.
answers.C: Use Amazon API Gateway with a usage plan and throttling limits to cap requests to the payment service; when limits are exceeded, API Gateway returns 429 errors to prevent cascade failures.
answers.D: Implement AWS Step Functions with a Wait state and retry logic to orchestrate calls to the payment service with exponential backoff at the workflow orchestration layer.

explanation: App Mesh with Envoy sidecars implements the circuit-breaker pattern transparently at the proxy layer—no application code changes needed. Envoy's outlier detection ejects unhealthy endpoints and its circuit-breaker limits pending requests. ALB health checks remove instances but don't implement circuit-breaker semantics (open/half-open/closed). API Gateway throttling protects the gateway, not the inter-service call path. Step Functions adds workflow orchestration but requires application-level changes.

stem: An e-commerce platform processes orders through a saga pattern spanning five microservices: Inventory, Payment, Shipping, Notification, and Fraud Detection. Each service must perform compensating transactions if any step fails. The system processes 500 orders/second at peak. Current implementation uses synchronous REST calls between services, causing tight coupling and timeouts. Which redesign minimizes coupling, supports compensation, and handles peak load?

answers.A: Use Amazon SQS FIFO queues between each service pair and implement dead-letter queues (DLQs) for failures. Each service polls its queue, processes the message, and enqueues the next service. Store saga state in DynamoDB.
answers.B: Implement an orchestration-based saga using AWS Step Functions Standard Workflow. Define each service call as a Task state with Catch blocks for failures and compensating Lambda functions. Use Express Workflows for high-throughput steps.
answers.C: Implement a choreography-based saga using Amazon EventBridge custom event bus. Each service publishes domain events; other services subscribe via EventBridge rules. Store saga state in DynamoDB with conditional writes for idempotency. Use SQS queues as EventBridge targets for backpressure.
answers.D: Use Amazon MQ with ActiveMQ to implement a message broker where each service subscribes to relevant topics. Implement compensating transactions via reply-to queues. Store inflight saga state in ElastiCache.

explanation: Choreography via EventBridge decouples services—each reacts to domain events without knowing other services. SQS as a target adds buffering for backpressure at 500 orders/second. DynamoDB with conditional writes ensures idempotency. Step Functions orchestration (B) centralizes logic but becomes a bottleneck at high throughput with Standard Workflows (which have cost and throughput limits vs Express); Express Workflows don't support async callbacks needed for external payment systems. SQS FIFO (A) maintains ordering but couples services via queue awareness. Amazon MQ adds operational complexity vs managed services.

stem: A company has 40 VPCs across 3 AWS Regions. Each VPC needs full mesh connectivity to every other VPC in all Regions. The network team also requires centralized inspection of all inter-VPC traffic through a firewall appliance, and a shared services VPC (DNS, patch management) that all other VPCs can access. Which architecture minimizes operational overhead while meeting all requirements?

answers.A: Create VPC peering connections between all VPCs in full mesh (780 peering connections). Route traffic through the shared services VPC for inspection by configuring the shared services VPC as a transit hub.
answers.B: Deploy an AWS Transit Gateway in each Region, peer the Transit Gateways inter-Region. Attach all VPCs to their regional TGW. Use VPC peering from the shared services VPC to each spoke VPC for DNS resolution.
answers.C: Deploy an AWS Transit Gateway in each Region with inter-Region peering. Attach all VPCs including a centralized inspection VPC containing the firewall appliance. Configure TGW route tables to send all inter-VPC traffic through the inspection VPC (appliance routing). Attach the shared services VPC to the TGW with a dedicated route table.
answers.D: Use AWS Cloud WAN with a global network policy to connect all VPCs. Deploy the firewall in a security segment and use Cloud WAN service insertion for traffic inspection. Share DNS via Route 53 Resolver endpoints in each VPC.

explanation: Transit Gateway with appliance routing in a centralized inspection VPC provides scalable full-mesh connectivity without the management overhead of 780 peering connections. Inter-Region TGW peering extends this globally. A dedicated inspection VPC with appliance mode TGW attachment ensures symmetric flows for stateful firewalls. Cloud WAN (D) is a valid newer approach but is more complex to configure; TGW is the well-established pattern. Full-mesh VPC peering (A) doesn't support transitive routing and becomes unmanageable at 40 VPCs.

stem: A SaaS vendor wants to expose an internal API service to 200 enterprise customer VPCs across different AWS accounts. The customers' VPCs may have overlapping CIDR ranges. The vendor wants to ensure customers can only call the API and cannot access any other resources in the vendor's VPC. Which connectivity model satisfies these requirements?

answers.A: Create an AWS PrivateLink endpoint service backed by a Network Load Balancer in the vendor's VPC. Each customer creates an interface VPC endpoint in their VPC. The vendor approves endpoint connections. Customers access the API via the endpoint DNS name.
answers.B: Establish VPC peering between the vendor's VPC and each customer VPC. Add route table entries for the vendor's API subnet in each customer VPC and restrict access with security groups.
answers.C: Deploy the API behind an internet-facing ALB with HTTPS. Issue each customer a unique API key for authentication. Use WAF to restrict access to known customer IP ranges.
answers.D: Create a Transit Gateway and share it with all customer accounts via AWS RAM. Attach the vendor VPC and all customer VPCs to the TGW. Use TGW route tables to permit only API subnet routes.

explanation: AWS PrivateLink is purpose-built for this scenario: it works across accounts with overlapping CIDRs, exposes only a specific service (not the full VPC), requires explicit vendor approval per customer, and keeps traffic on the AWS network. VPC peering (B) fails with overlapping CIDRs and gives broader network visibility. Internet-facing ALB (C) doesn't provide private connectivity. Transit Gateway (D) requires non-overlapping CIDRs and exposes the full VPC routing domain unless extensively segmented.
tags: Determine high-performing and/or scalable network architectures
Network connection options (for example, AWS VPN, AWS Direct Connect, AWS PrivateLink)
How to design network architecture (for example, subnet tiers, routing, IP addressing)
Determining network segmentation strategies (for example, using public subnets and private subnets)

stem: A financial trading platform requires an RTO of < 1 minute and RPO of 0 (zero data loss) across an entire AWS Region failure. The application is stateful with DynamoDB as the primary database, an ElastiCache Redis cluster for session state, and EC2-based trading engines that must process in order. Which architecture achieves these requirements?

answers.A: Use DynamoDB Global Tables for multi-Region replication. Set up a warm standby with EC2 Auto Scaling in the secondary Region scaled to 25% capacity. Use Route 53 health checks with failover routing. Accept eventual consistency for session state by using a shared DynamoDB table for sessions.
answers.B: Use DynamoDB Global Tables (multi-active) for zero-RPO database replication. Use ElastiCache Global Datastore for Redis to replicate session state. Run active trading engines in both Regions behind Route 53 latency-based routing. Use a distributed lock (DynamoDB conditional writes) to manage order sequencing. Configure Route 53 health checks with failover to handle Region failure.
answers.C: Use Aurora Global Database with a primary in Region A and a read replica in Region B. Promote the replica on failure (typical RPO < 1 second but not zero). Use ElastiCache read replicas in Region B. Set RTO by pre-warming EC2 in Region B using Auto Scaling scheduled actions.
answers.D: Deploy the application in two Regions with AWS Global Accelerator directing traffic. Use S3 Cross-Region Replication for session state and DynamoDB Streams to replicate data to a secondary Region DynamoDB table using Lambda.

explanation: DynamoDB Global Tables provides multi-active, multi-Region replication with near-zero RPO (sub-second replication). ElastiCache Global Datastore replicates Redis with ~1-second latency between Regions. Running active engines in both Regions with Route 53 latency routing achieves sub-1-minute RTO (no warmup needed). Conditional writes handle sequencing. Option A uses warm standby (not active-active) with a 1-minute+ startup time. Aurora Global DB has a ~1-second RPO, not zero. S3 for session state (D) doesn't provide the required consistency or latency.

stem: A healthcare company runs a critical patient records application on EC2 (m5.4xlarge, 16 instances), RDS MySQL Multi-AZ, and EFS. The business requires RTO ≤ 4 hours and RPO ≤ 15 minutes. The annual IT budget for DR is $50,000. Current monthly spend in the primary Region is $28,000. Which DR strategy fits within budget while meeting the RTO/RPO requirements?

answers.A: Active-active multi-Region with full capacity in the secondary Region, Route 53 active-active routing, and DynamoDB Global Tables for state. Estimated monthly DR cost: $28,000.
answers.B: Warm standby with 25% capacity (4 instances) running 24/7 in secondary Region, RDS read replica promoted on failure, EFS replication. Estimated monthly DR cost: ~$9,000.
answers.C: Pilot light with a stopped Auto Scaling group (launch template configured) and an RDS read replica in the secondary Region. Enable EFS replication. Use AWS Backup for point-in-time recovery. On failure, scale the ASG to 16 instances and promote the read replica. Estimated monthly DR cost: ~$2,500.
answers.D: Backup and restore using AWS Backup for EC2 AMIs (every 15 minutes), RDS automated snapshots, and EFS backups. Store backups cross-Region. On failure, restore from backup. Estimated monthly DR cost: ~$500.

explanation: Pilot light keeps the RDS read replica (near-real-time replication meets 15-min RPO) and replicates EFS continuously. On failure, ASG launch with pre-baked AMIs and RDS promotion typically completes in 1-2 hours, meeting the 4-hour RTO. At ~$2,500/month ($30,000/year) it's within budget. Backup and restore (D) is cheapest but restoring 16 instances from snapshots plus RDS typically takes 4-8 hours, exceeding RTO. Warm standby (B) at $9,000/month ($108,000/year) exceeds the $50,000 budget. Active-active (A) costs $336,000/year.

stem: A BI team uses Amazon QuickSight with a 500 GB dataset in Amazon Redshift. Dashboard load times are 15-25 seconds due to complex Redshift queries. The data is updated hourly. The team has 300 concurrent users during business hours. The BI team wants to reduce dashboard load times to under 3 seconds without significant infrastructure changes. SPICE capacity is available. Which approach achieves this?

answers.A: Import the dataset into SPICE using a scheduled refresh every hour. SPICE's in-memory engine serves queries in milliseconds, reducing dashboard load times well under 3 seconds. The 300 concurrent users all benefit from the cached dataset.
answers.B: Switch from Redshift to Amazon Athena as the QuickSight data source. Athena's serverless query engine scales automatically and provides faster responses than Redshift for BI queries.
answers.C: Enable Redshift concurrency scaling to handle 300 concurrent users. Add read replicas to the Redshift cluster. Configure QuickSight to use direct query mode to always fetch fresh data.
answers.D: Configure QuickSight to use Amazon ElastiCache for Redis as a query cache layer. Point QuickSight at ElastiCache; on cache miss, ElastiCache fetches from Redshift and returns results.

explanation: SPICE (Super-fast Parallel In-memory Calculation Engine) caches the dataset in QuickSight's in-memory store and serves all 300 concurrent users from it, achieving sub-second query times. Hourly refresh keeps data current. Athena (B) still issues SQL queries to S3 and won't match SPICE's latency. Redshift concurrency scaling (C) helps throughput but 15-25 second query time is a query complexity issue, not concurrency. QuickSight doesn't support ElastiCache as a data source (D).
tags: Determine high-performing data ingestion and transformation solutions
Caching strategies and services (for example, Amazon ElastiCache)
Data access patterns (for example, read-intensive compared with write-intensive)
Integrating caching to meet business requirements

stem: A company wants to sync Salesforce Opportunity records to Amazon S3 for analytics. New and updated records must reach S3 within 5 minutes. The data contains PII that must be encrypted at rest using a customer-managed KMS key, and certain sensitive fields (SSN, credit card numbers) must be masked before storage. The solution must require no custom code. Which AppFlow configuration satisfies these requirements?

answers.A: Create an AppFlow flow with Salesforce as source and S3 as destination, triggered on a 5-minute schedule. Enable S3 SSE-S3 encryption. Use a post-flow Lambda function to mask sensitive fields after the files land in S3.
answers.B: Create an AppFlow flow with event-based trigger (Salesforce Platform Events). Use data masking in the AppFlow field mapping. Store output in S3 with SSE-KMS using the default AWS-managed key.
answers.C: Create an AppFlow flow with Salesforce Change Data Capture (CDC) or event-based trigger for near-real-time delivery. In the flow's field mapping, apply masking transforms to sensitive fields. Configure the S3 destination with a customer-managed KMS key for SSE-KMS encryption.
answers.D: Create an AppFlow flow triggered every 5 minutes using incremental export (filter on LastModifiedDate > last run). Write results to an S3 bucket. Use S3 default encryption with SSE-KMS (AWS-managed key). Deploy a Glue job to mask fields as a post-processing step.

explanation: AppFlow natively supports field-level masking transforms (e.g., mask, truncate, concatenate) configured in the flow's field mapping—no custom code needed. Event-based or CDC triggers enable near-real-time (<5 min) delivery. Specifying a customer-managed KMS key in the S3 destination config satisfies the CMK requirement. Option A uses a Lambda for masking (custom code). Option B uses AWS-managed key, not CMK. Option D uses a Glue job for masking (custom code) and misses the CMK requirement.
tags: Determine high-performing data ingestion and transformation solutions
Data transformation services with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS Glue)
Encrypting data at rest (for example, AWS KMS)

stem: A company runs a custom on-premises CRM system with a REST API accessible only from within their corporate network (connected to AWS via AWS Direct Connect). They want to use Amazon AppFlow to pull customer data from the CRM into Amazon Redshift for analysis. The CRM API cannot be exposed to the public internet. Which configuration enables AppFlow to access the private CRM endpoint?

answers.A: Create a custom AppFlow connector using the AppFlow Connector SDK. Deploy it as a public internet-facing API so AppFlow can reach it from the AWS managed service network.
answers.B: Use AppFlow's private connectivity option with a PrivateLink-based VPC interface endpoint. Deploy an AppFlow custom connector or use the on-premises profile with a private endpoint that routes through Direct Connect to the CRM.
answers.C: Set up a Site-to-Site VPN from the on-premises CRM network to a VPC. Deploy a reverse proxy (EC2 Nginx) in the VPC that forwards requests to the CRM. Point AppFlow at the public IP of the proxy.
answers.D: Use AWS DataSync with a DataSync agent installed on-premises to replicate CRM REST API responses to S3, then use AppFlow with S3 as the source to load into Redshift.

explanation: AppFlow supports private connectivity via AWS PrivateLink, allowing flows to reach endpoints in private VPCs (and by extension, on-premises resources over Direct Connect or VPN through a VPC). This keeps all traffic off the public internet. A public proxy (C) exposes the CRM to the internet. DataSync (D) is designed for file/object transfer, not REST API data extraction. The custom connector deployed publicly (A) defeats the private connectivity requirement.
tags: Network connection options (for example, AWS VPN, AWS Direct Connect, AWS PrivateLink)
Securing external network connections to and from the AWS Cloud (for example, VPN, AWS Direct Connect)

stem: A collaborative document editing app uses AWS AppSync GraphQL API with DynamoDB as the data source. When one user saves a document, all other users currently viewing the same document must receive the update in real time. The app uses Amazon Cognito User Pools for authentication. Updates must only be delivered to users who have permission to view the specific document. Which AppSync configuration achieves per-document authorization for real-time updates?

answers.A: Define a GraphQL subscription with a documentId argument. In the AppSync subscription resolver, use an AWS Lambda authorizer that verifies the requesting user's Cognito claims against a permissions table in DynamoDB. AppSync delivers subscription events only to connected clients subscribed to the matching documentId.
answers.B: Use AppSync with AWS_IAM authorization. Attach an IAM policy to each Cognito identity pool role that grants appsync:Subscribe on a specific documentId ARN pattern. AppSync enforces the IAM policy for each subscription connection.
answers.C: Configure AppSync to use OPENID_CONNECT authorization. Embed documentId permissions in the JWT claims. Write a resolver that validates the JWT and filters subscription events based on claims.
answers.D: Use AppSync with API_KEY authorization for subscriptions. Generate a unique API key per document and distribute it to authorized users. Clients include the key when subscribing; AppSync validates the key.

explanation: AppSync subscription filters allow server-side filtering of events to subscribed clients. A Lambda authorizer can inspect Cognito claims and the requested documentId to allow/deny the subscription connection. AppSync then only delivers events matching the subscribed documentId argument to authorized clients. AWS_IAM (B) can't dynamically scope permissions per document-ID at subscription time without very complex IAM conditions. OIDC (C) with embedded claims requires claims to encode every accessible document, which doesn't scale. API keys (D) are not per-user and provide no user-level authorization.
tags: AWS federated access and identity services (for example, IAM, AWS IAM Identity Center)
Security services with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS Cognito, AWS GuardDuty, AWS Macie)
Integrating AWS services to secure applications (for example, AWS Shield, AWS WAF, IAM Identity Center, AWS Secrets Manager)

stem: A developer is building a SAM application that needs to use a pre-built authentication component published in the AWS Serverless Application Repository. The authentication component requires two parameters: CallbackURL and AllowedOAuthScopes. The developer's application must pass its own API Gateway endpoint URL as the CallbackURL. The API Gateway URL is only known after deployment. How should the developer integrate the SAR nested application?

answers.A: Reference the SAR application as a nested application resource (AWS::Serverless::Application) in the parent SAM template. Use the !GetAtt nested stack output for the auth component's ARNs. For the CallbackURL, pass the API Gateway URL as a parameter using !Sub or !Join with a !Ref to the API Gateway resource in the same template.
answers.B: Deploy the SAR authentication component separately first. Note its outputs, then hardcode those values as parameters in the main SAM template. Deploy the main application as a second step.
answers.C: Use a CloudFormation Custom Resource backed by a Lambda function that deploys the SAR application at runtime and returns the authentication component's outputs for use by other resources.
answers.D: Export the authentication component's parameters from SAR to SSM Parameter Store during the SAR deployment. In the main template, use dynamic SSM parameter references ({{resolve:ssm:/auth/callback}}) for the CallbackURL.

explanation: SAM natively supports nested applications via AWS::Serverless::Application, which creates a nested CloudFormation stack. You can pass outputs from one resource as inputs to another within the same template, including dynamically resolved values like API Gateway URLs using !Sub or !Ref. This is the clean, single-deployment approach. Two-stage deployments (B) are operationally cumbersome and break infrastructure-as-code atomicity. Custom Resources (C) add complexity unnecessarily. SSM dynamic references (D) only work if the SAR application explicitly writes to SSM, which the auth component doesn't.
tags: Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
Serverless technologies and patterns (for example, AWS Fargate, AWS Lambda)
API creation and management (for example, Amazon API Gateway, REST API)
Determining when to use serverless technologies and patterns

stem: A retail company deploys containerized point-of-sale applications on servers in 500 store locations using Amazon ECS Anywhere. Each store's external instance must pull container images from Amazon ECR and write transaction logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. The external instances have no IAM roles since they are not EC2 instances. What is the correct approach to grant the external instances the necessary AWS permissions?

answers.A: Install the SSM Agent and ECS Agent on each external instance. During ECS Anywhere registration, AWS Systems Manager creates a managed instance with an associated IAM role. Attach a custom IAM role to the ECS task definition with permissions for ECR and CloudWatch Logs. Grant the managed instance role permissions for SSM and ECS registration.
answers.B: Generate long-term IAM access keys for an IAM user with ECR and CloudWatch Logs permissions. Distribute the keys to each external instance via environment variables in the ECS task definition.
answers.C: Use IAM roles for EC2 instances: assign an instance profile to each external server and attach policies for ECR, CloudWatch Logs, and SSM. ECS Anywhere will discover the instance profile automatically.
answers.D: Create an S3 bucket with a bucket policy granting public read access to container images. Export CloudWatch Logs to S3 and sync from external instances using the AWS CLI with embedded credentials.

explanation: ECS Anywhere uses AWS Systems Manager to manage external instances. During registration (ecs create-activation, ssm register-managed-instance), a managed instance activation is created and the SSM Agent enables the instance to authenticate with AWS. Task-level permissions are handled through the ECS task IAM role, just as with EC2. The managed instance role covers SSM/ECS agent communication. Long-term access keys (B) are a security anti-pattern. Instance profiles (C) are for EC2 only. Public S3 for images (D) is a security violation.

AWS federated access and identity services (for example, IAM, AWS IAM Identity Center)
The orchestration of containers (for example, Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS)

stem: A defense contractor runs Kubernetes workloads in a classified environment with no internet connectivity and strict requirements that all software bills of materials (SBOM) be reviewed before use. They need a Kubernetes distribution where they can control every component version, run in a fully air-gapped environment, and use their own internal container registry. Which AWS Kubernetes offering best fits this scenario?

answers.A: Amazon EKS managed node groups: configure the EKS cluster in a private VPC with PrivateLink endpoints, push all required images to an ECR Private repository, and use VPC endpoints for all AWS service traffic.
answers.B: Amazon EKS Anywhere on bare metal: deploy EKS Anywhere in the classified environment. Configure airgap installation, using an internal registry mirror (Harbor) to host all required container images and Helm charts.
answers.C: Amazon EKS Distro (EKS-D): download the EKS-D source and binary artifacts. Run the components on bare metal or VMs in the classified environment using a self-managed Kubernetes installation. Mirror all container images to an internal registry and build a completely disconnected control plane.
answers.D: Deploy upstream Kubernetes using kubeadm in the classified environment. Use EKS-D manifests only as a reference for component versions. Manage upgrades and SBOMs manually.

explanation: EKS Distro (EKS-D) provides the same Kubernetes components used in EKS but as downloadable artifacts you fully control, making it ideal for air-gapped classified environments where all SBOMs must be reviewed. EKS Anywhere (B) is also air-gap capable but requires the EKS Anywhere cluster controller, which has additional cloud dependencies; EKS-D gives even more direct control. Managed EKS (A) requires AWS control plane connectivity. Upstream Kubernetes (D) abandons the AWS-maintained SBOM and distribution benefits.
tags: The orchestration of containers (for example, Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS)
How to migrate applications into containers
AWS security best practices (for example, the principle of least privilege)

stem: A gaming company uses Amazon Keyspaces to store player event data. The table schema is: PRIMARY KEY (game_id, event_time) with game_id as the partition key. A viral new game generates 90% of all write traffic to a single game_id, causing throttling even with on-demand capacity mode. The architecture team must eliminate the hotspot without changing the application's query patterns (queries filter by game_id and event_time range). Which schema change resolves this?

answers.A: Switch the primary key to (event_time, game_id) so that event_time is the partition key. This distributes writes across time-based partitions.
answers.B: Add a shard suffix column: PRIMARY KEY ((game_id, shard), event_time). Compute shard = random int 0-9 at write time. At read time, query all 10 shards for the given game_id in parallel and merge results client-side.
answers.C: Enable Keyspaces auto-scaling to increase throughput capacity on demand. Set the target utilization to 50% to allow headroom for spikes.
answers.D: Enable Keyspaces point-in-time recovery (PITR) and configure read replicas in multiple Regions to distribute the read load away from the hot partition.

explanation: The hotspot is caused by all writes for the viral game going to one Cassandra partition. Sharding by adding a random shard to the partition key distributes writes across 10 partitions. Reads query all shards in parallel and merge. This is the standard Cassandra hot-partition mitigation. Swapping to event_time as partition key (A) creates time-based hotspots (all current writes go to the same time bucket). Auto-scaling (C) doesn't help with a partition-level hotspot—Keyspaces can't split a single partition. PITR and read replicas (D) address read scalability, not write hotspots.

Data access patterns (for example, read-intensive compared with write-intensive)
Scalability capabilities with appropriate use cases (for example, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling, AWS Auto Scaling)

stem: A fraud detection team needs to build a graph database in Amazon Neptune to model financial transaction relationships. They have two query requirements: (1) Find all accounts within 3 hops of a flagged account that share a device fingerprint or IP address (traversal query); (2) Query the graph using SPARQL to integrate with an existing RDF knowledge graph used by the compliance team. The development team is more experienced with property graphs. Which approach best meets both requirements?

answers.A: Create two separate Neptune clusters: one with property graph (Gremlin) for traversal queries and one with RDF (SPARQL) for the compliance knowledge graph. Use a Lambda function to synchronize data between them.
answers.B: Use only Gremlin (TinkerPop) on a single Neptune cluster. Write a custom Lambda function to translate SPARQL queries from the compliance team into equivalent Gremlin traversals.
answers.C: Amazon Neptune supports both Gremlin (property graph) and SPARQL (RDF) on the same cluster simultaneously. Model the fraud graph as a property graph and use Gremlin for traversal queries; load the RDF knowledge graph using the Neptune bulk loader and query with SPARQL—both on the same Neptune cluster.
answers.D: Use Amazon Neptune Analytics (graph analytics on vector-based graph) for traversal queries and Neptune database for SPARQL. Use Neptune Federation to join query results.

explanation: Amazon Neptune supports both the property graph model (queried with Gremlin/openCypher) and RDF (queried with SPARQL) on the same cluster. Teams can use Gremlin for property graph traversals and SPARQL for RDF, even loading and querying both data models within one cluster. No need for separate clusters or translation layers. Neptune Analytics (D) is a separate service for graph analytics (algorithms like PageRank, shortest path at scale) and doesn't eliminate the need for the SPARQL RDF model.
tags: Database types and services (for example, serverless, relational compared with non-relational, in-memory)
Determining an appropriate database type (for example, Amazon Aurora, Amazon DynamoDB)

stem: A healthcare company processes insurance claim forms using Amazon Textract. The forms vary in layout across 20 insurance providers, making key-value pair extraction unreliable (the same field appears in different positions and with different labels across forms). The team needs to reliably extract 10 specific fields (patient name, date of birth, diagnosis code, claim amount, etc.) regardless of form layout. Which Textract capability should they use?

answers.A: Use AnalyzeDocument with FORMS feature type and post-process key-value pairs using fuzzy matching on key names to identify the 10 target fields.
answers.B: Use AnalyzeDocument with LAYOUT feature type to identify document structure, then write custom parsing logic to locate each field based on spatial coordinates.
answers.C: Use AnalyzeDocument with the QUERIES feature type. Define 10 natural language queries (e.g., 'What is the patient name?', 'What is the diagnosis code?'). Textract uses ML to locate and extract the answer regardless of its position or label in the document.
answers.D: Train a custom Amazon Rekognition model to identify and extract the 10 specific fields from the claim form images based on their expected positions in a reference layout.

explanation: Amazon Textract Queries allow users to ask specific natural language questions about a document, and Textract's ML model finds the answer regardless of where it appears or how the label is worded. This is specifically designed for layout-variable documents where FORMS-based key-value extraction fails due to label inconsistency. Fuzzy matching on FORMS output (A) is fragile and requires maintenance. LAYOUT-based spatial parsing (B) requires complex custom logic. Rekognition (D) is for image recognition, not structured document extraction.
tags: AWS Managed Services (AMS) with appropriate use cases (for example, Amazon Comprehend, Amazon Polly)
Data transformation services with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS Glue)

stem: A company's security policy requires that every new AWS account provisioned through AWS Control Tower's Account Factory must: (1) have a specific VPC configuration with private/public subnets in 3 AZs deployed; (2) have AWS Security Hub enabled with CIS Level 1 standard; (3) have an IAM role for the central security team with read-only access. These requirements must be enforced automatically without human intervention for each new account. Which implementation is correct?

answers.A: After each account is created, trigger a Lambda function via EventBridge (on the CreateManagedAccount Control Tower lifecycle event) that assumes a cross-account role and deploys the VPC, Security Hub, and IAM role using CloudFormation.
answers.B: Create a Service Control Policy that enforces the VPC configuration. Use a detective guardrail to verify Security Hub is enabled. Manually create the IAM role template and notify account owners to deploy it.
answers.C: Use Control Tower Account Factory Customizations (CfCT) with a CloudFormation template defining the VPC, Security Hub enablement (AWS::SecurityHub::Hub), and the IAM role. CfCT automatically applies the template to each new account during provisioning.
answers.D: Configure Account Factory for Terraform (AFT) or CfCT with a customization pipeline that applies Terraform/CloudFormation templates for the VPC, Security Hub, and IAM role as part of the account vending workflow. This runs automatically for every account provisioned through Account Factory.

explanation: CfCT (Customizations for Control Tower) and AFT both integrate with the Account Factory provisioning pipeline to automatically apply CloudFormation/Terraform templates to every new account—VPC, Security Hub, IAM roles—without manual intervention. EventBridge Lambda (A) works but is more fragile (Lambda failures silently skip customization) and is a custom solution vs. the purpose-built CfCT/AFT. SCPs (B) can't create resources; they only restrict actions. CfCT (C) is correct but D emphasizes the full AFT/CfCT pipeline pattern, which is the complete answer.
tags: Design secure access to AWS resources
Access controls and management across multiple accounts
AWS security best practices (for example, the principle of least privilege)
Designing a security strategy for multiple AWS accounts (for example, AWS Control Tower, service control policies [SCPs])

stem: A cloud platform team uses AWS Service Catalog to offer a portfolio of approved EC2 and RDS products to development teams. Development teams should be able to launch products without needing IAM permissions to directly call ec2:RunInstances or rds:CreateDBInstance. However, all launched products must be tagged with a CostCenter tag matching the team's budget code. Which Service Catalog configuration enforces both requirements?

answers.A: Add the development teams' IAM roles to the portfolio and grant AmazonEC2FullAccess and AmazonRDSFullAccess managed policies. Configure an AWS Config rule to detect missing CostCenter tags post-launch.
answers.B: Use a Launch Constraint: associate an IAM role with the catalog product that has ec2:RunInstances and rds:CreateDBInstance permissions. Add a tag update Lambda triggered by Config to retroactively add missing tags.
answers.C: Configure a Launch Constraint IAM role in Service Catalog with the necessary EC2/RDS permissions. The end user's IAM role only needs servicecatalog:ProvisionProduct permission. Add a TagOption to the portfolio requiring the CostCenter tag; Service Catalog propagates the TagOption to all provisioned products.
answers.D: Use an SCP to deny ec2:RunInstances unless the request includes the CostCenter tag condition. Grant development teams AmazonEC2FullAccess directly. Service Catalog is unnecessary for tag enforcement.

explanation: Service Catalog Launch Constraints specify an IAM role that Service Catalog assumes to provision the product, so end users don't need direct EC2/RDS IAM permissions—they only need servicecatalog:ProvisionProduct. TagOptions enforce mandatory tags across all provisioned products in the portfolio and are propagated automatically. Config retroactive tagging (B) doesn't prevent missing tags at launch. SCPs + direct access (D) bypasses the purpose of Service Catalog and doesn't provide product governance.
tags: Design secure access to AWS resources
AWS security best practices (for example, the principle of least privilege)
Designing a flexible authorization model that includes IAM users, groups, roles, and policies
Determining the appropriate use of resource policies for AWS services

stem: An oil and gas company operates a remote drilling site with no reliable internet connectivity. They need to: (1) collect and process real-time sensor data from 200 IoT devices using a containerized ML inference application; (2) store 60 TB of raw sensor data locally for 30 days before shipping to AWS; (3) run EC2 instances on-site for a SCADA monitoring dashboard. Which AWS Snow Family device is appropriate?

answers.A: Order an AWS Snowcone. It provides 8 TB of storage, 2 vCPUs, 4 GB RAM—sufficient for IoT collection, local storage, and the SCADA dashboard.
answers.B: Order an AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device (80 TB usable storage, limited compute). This provides the storage capacity and basic compute for sensor data collection.
answers.C: Order an AWS Snowball Edge Compute Optimized device (28 TB NVMe usable storage + 42 TB HDD, 52 vCPUs, 208 GB RAM, optional GPU). It supports EC2 instances, ECS containers for ML inference, and S3-compatible local storage for 60 TB raw data.
answers.D: Order an AWS Snowmobile. It provides exabyte-scale storage capacity suitable for large-scale data collection and has built-in compute for edge processing.

explanation: Snowball Edge Compute Optimized provides substantial compute (52 vCPUs, 208 GB RAM) for running EC2 instances and ECS containers (ML inference), plus 28 TB NVMe + 42 TB HDD (~70 TB total) for the 60 TB storage requirement. It supports all three use cases. Snowcone (A) has insufficient storage (8 TB) and compute. Snowball Edge Storage Optimized (B) has limited compute (24 vCPUs) and may struggle with EC2 + containers + ML simultaneously. Snowmobile (D) is a truck-mounted storage service for 10+ PB, with no edge compute capability.
tags: Determine high-performing and/or scalable storage solutions
AWS compute services with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS Batch, Amazon EMR, AWS Fargate)
Hybrid storage solutions to meet business requirements

stem: Amazon GuardDuty generates frequent 'S3/AnomalousBehavior' findings because a data engineering pipeline's IAM role regularly scans thousands of S3 prefixes as part of its normal workflow. The security team validates these are false positives for this specific role but wants to keep GuardDuty findings for all other principals. The security team wants to suppress these false positives automatically without disabling GuardDuty or S3 Protection. Which GuardDuty feature should be used?

answers.A: Create a GuardDuty suppression rule that filters on finding type 'S3/AnomalousBehavior' AND resource.accessKeyDetails.principalId matching the data engineering IAM role ARN. Suppressed findings are not published to Security Hub or EventBridge and don't count against finding limits.
answers.B: Add the data engineering IAM role's ARN to the GuardDuty trusted IP list. GuardDuty will not generate findings for traffic originating from trusted IP addresses.
answers.C: Create a GuardDuty filter that tags the findings from this role as 'Archived' using the UpdateFindings API called by a Lambda function triggered by EventBridge on each finding.
answers.D: Disable GuardDuty S3 Protection for the specific S3 buckets accessed by the data engineering pipeline. This prevents GuardDuty from analyzing events for those buckets.

explanation: GuardDuty suppression rules permanently archive matching findings before they are published—they never appear in the console, Security Hub, or EventBridge. This is the correct mechanism for managing known false positives without affecting other principals. Trusted IP lists (B) are based on IP addresses, not IAM principals, and are used for reducing findings from known safe IP ranges, not role-specific suppression. Lambda archiving via EventBridge (C) is a manual workaround that still generates and publishes the finding before archiving. Disabling S3 Protection per bucket (D) removes detection for all principals accessing those buckets, not just the data engineering role.

stem: A financial services company uses Amazon Macie to scan S3 buckets for sensitive data. Macie's managed identifiers find standard PII (SSNs, credit card numbers) but miss the company's proprietary customer identifiers (format: CUS-[9 digits]) and internal account codes (format: ACCT-[A-Z]{2}-[0-9]{6}). The compliance team needs Macie to flag these identifiers as high-severity sensitive data. Which Macie feature addresses this?

answers.A: Add the proprietary patterns to Macie's allowlist. Macie will treat them as known non-sensitive data and stop flagging them (inverse of requirement—this suppresses findings).
answers.B: Create Macie Custom Data Identifiers with regex patterns matching each format: CUS-\d{9} and ACCT-[A-Z]{2}-\d{6}. Set the keyword proximity and maximum match distance as needed. Configure a sensitivity score for each identifier. Macie applies custom identifiers alongside managed ones in discovery jobs.
answers.C: Enable Macie automated sensitive data discovery on all S3 buckets. Macie's ML models will learn the proprietary identifier patterns from historical data without explicit configuration.
answers.D: Write a Lambda function that scans S3 objects using regex and publishes findings to Security Hub. Use Security Hub's aggregation to combine with Macie findings in a unified view.

explanation: Macie Custom Data Identifiers allow users to define regex patterns (with optional keywords for proximity matching) to detect organization-specific sensitive data formats. These run alongside managed identifiers in discovery jobs and appear in Macie findings with configurable severity. Allowlists (A) suppress findings rather than creating them. Macie's ML doesn't auto-learn new identifier formats from data (C)—custom identifiers require explicit definition. Lambda + Security Hub (D) adds custom code and doesn't leverage Macie's native sensitive data discovery workflows.
tags: Security services with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS Cognito, AWS GuardDuty, AWS Macie)

stem: A company wants to run Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery across all S3 buckets in a production account. They have 500 buckets, 10 TB of total data, and a monthly Macie budget of $2,000. Macie pricing is $1/GB for the first 50 GB per month (sensitive data discovery), with tiered pricing beyond that. They want to prioritize scanning of buckets likely to contain PII (tagged DataClass=Sensitive) first, and scan other buckets only if budget remains. Which configuration achieves this?

answers.A: Create two Macie sensitive data discovery jobs: Job 1 with a bucket filter for tag DataClass=Sensitive, scheduled to run first with no object size limit. Monitor Macie usage costs via CloudWatch metrics. Create Job 2 for untagged buckets scheduled after Job 1 completes with an object size limit to stay within budget.
answers.B: Enable Macie automated sensitive data discovery, which uses ML to prioritize buckets with likely sensitive data. Set a cost budget in AWS Budgets to alert when $2,000 is reached and manually pause Macie.
answers.C: Run Macie one-time discovery jobs on all 500 buckets simultaneously. Use S3 object sampling (10% of objects per bucket) to reduce cost. This covers all buckets while staying under $2,000.
answers.D: Configure Macie to scan only the most recently modified objects (last 30 days) across all buckets. Use S3 Storage Lens to identify high-activity buckets and create a Macie managed job targeting those buckets.

explanation: Creating separate jobs with bucket-level filters (tag-based) controls which buckets Macie scans and in what order. Job 1 covers sensitive-tagged buckets; Job 2 covers the remainder with object limits for budget control. CloudWatch Macie usage metrics help monitor spend. Automated sensitive data discovery (B) doesn't provide fine-grained budget control and can't be configured to scan tagged buckets first. Sampling all 500 buckets simultaneously (C) doesn't prioritize sensitive buckets. S3 Storage Lens (D) identifies activity but doesn't control Macie scan prioritization.
tags: Security services with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS Cognito, AWS GuardDuty, AWS Macie)

stem: A company is migrating a containerized application from an on-premises Kubernetes cluster to Amazon ECS on Fargate. The application has 5 microservices, each with its own Docker image. The images are currently in an on-premises Docker registry. The team needs a CI/CD pipeline that builds new images on code commit, stores them securely, and deploys to ECS with a blue/green deployment strategy to minimize downtime. Which AWS services fulfill these requirements?

answers.A: Use AWS CodeCommit for source control, CodeBuild to build and push images to DockerHub, and CodeDeploy with an ECS deployment group for blue/green. Configure ECS services to pull from DockerHub using stored credentials in Secrets Manager.
answers.B: Use AWS CodePipeline orchestrating: CodeBuild to build Docker images and push to Amazon ECR; CodeDeploy with an ECS deployment group configured for blue/green (using ALB target groups to shift traffic). ECR provides image scanning and lifecycle policies. ECS Fargate pulls images from ECR using task execution role permissions.
answers.C: Use GitHub Actions to build and push images to ECR. Use AWS CloudFormation with Rolling update deployment type to update the ECS service. Blue/green is achieved by maintaining two ECS services (blue and green) and manually switching ALB target groups.
answers.D: Use AWS Elastic Beanstalk with multi-container Docker platform. Beanstalk handles image registry, CI/CD, and deployment strategy natively. All 5 microservices run as a single Beanstalk environment.

explanation: CodePipeline + CodeBuild + ECR + CodeDeploy is the AWS-native CI/CD stack for containerized applications. ECR provides private, IAM-authenticated image storage with vulnerability scanning. CodeDeploy ECS blue/green deployment uses two ALB target groups to route traffic between old (blue) and new (green) task sets, shifting traffic gradually with automatic rollback on failures. DockerHub (A) is public and requires credential management. GitHub Actions + manual ALB switching (C) lacks automated rollback. Elastic Beanstalk (D) is not designed for multi-service microarchitecture at this granularity.

stem: A VPC has CIDR 10.0.0.0/16. A subnet's route table has three routes: (1) 10.0.0.0/16 → local; (2) 0.0.0.0/0 → igw-xxx (internet gateway); (3) 10.0.1.0/24 → tgw-xxx (Transit Gateway). An EC2 instance in this subnet sends a packet to 10.0.1.50. Which route is selected and why?

answers.A: Route (1) is selected (10.0.0.0/16 → local) because the destination falls within the VPC CIDR and local routes always take precedence over all other routes.
answers.B: Route (2) is selected (0.0.0.0/0 → igw) because the default route covers all destinations not matched by a more specific route, and 10.0.1.50 doesn't match the /24.
answers.C: Route (3) is selected (10.0.1.0/24 → tgw-xxx) because it is the most specific route matching 10.0.1.50 (longest prefix match). In AWS VPC routing, more specific prefix matches override the local route for propagated or static routes that overlap the VPC CIDR.
answers.D: The packet is dropped because conflicting routes (local and TGW) for the same prefix create an ambiguous routing decision, and VPC route tables don't support route priorities.

explanation: AWS VPC route tables use longest-prefix match. 10.0.1.0/24 is more specific than 10.0.0.0/16 (longer prefix = /24 > /16), so route (3) matches for 10.0.1.50. AWS supports adding more-specific routes for prefixes within the VPC CIDR to route traffic to TGW, VPN, or other targets—this is a common pattern for hybrid connectivity. The local route is not always highest priority when more specific routes exist. Route (2) (0.0.0.0/0) is least specific and only used when no other route matches.

stem: An application stores versioned objects in an S3 bucket with versioning enabled. The lifecycle requirements are: (1) current versions should move to S3 Intelligent-Tiering after 30 days; (2) non-current versions should move to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after 60 days and expire (delete) after 365 days; (3) delete markers for objects with no remaining versions should be automatically removed. Which S3 lifecycle configuration achieves all requirements?

answers.A: Create a lifecycle rule with: (a) Transition current versions to S3 Intelligent-Tiering after 30 days; (b) Transition non-current versions to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after 60 days; (c) Expire non-current versions after 365 days; (d) Enable the 'Expire current versions' or 'Clean up expired object delete markers' option. S3 automatically removes delete markers with no remaining versions when this is enabled.
answers.B: Create two separate lifecycle rules: one for current versions (transition to Intelligent-Tiering at 30 days) and one for non-current versions (transition to Glacier at 60 days, expire at 365 days). Delete markers must be removed manually via a Lambda function.
answers.C: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering for the entire bucket (bucket-level configuration) to automatically manage all tiers. Configure non-current version expiration via a lifecycle rule. Delete markers can only be removed by disabling versioning.
answers.D: Use S3 Replication to copy current versions to a separate bucket with Intelligent-Tiering configured. Keep non-current versions in the source bucket and apply glacier transition and expiration via lifecycle rules. Configure S3 Batch Operations to remove delete markers monthly.

explanation: S3 lifecycle rules support all three requirements in a single rule: current version transitions, non-current version transitions and expirations, and the 'Expire current versions'/'Clean up expired object delete markers' option for automatic delete marker cleanup. Two rules (B) work but the delete marker cleanup is native, not requiring Lambda. Bucket-level Intelligent-Tiering (C) applies to objects but doesn't handle the versioning-specific requirements, and you can't remove delete markers just by disabling versioning. Replication (D) adds unnecessary complexity.
tags: Storage tiering (for example, cold tiering for object storage)
Storage services with appropriate use cases (for example, Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon EBS)
Selecting the correct data lifecycle for storage

stem: A company in Account A stores sensitive data in S3 encrypted with a KMS customer-managed key (CMK) in Account A. A data processing application running in Account B needs to decrypt and process this data. The security team requires: (1) Account B cannot use the CMK for any purpose other than decryption; (2) the CMK cannot be deleted or key rotation disabled by Account B; (3) access can be revoked instantly. Which IAM/KMS configuration achieves this?

answers.A: Share the CMK with Account B by adding Account B's root ARN to the KMS key policy with kms:Decrypt, kms:GenerateDataKey, kms:DescribeKey, and kms:* permissions. Account B creates an IAM role with kms:* on the shared key.
answers.B: Generate a data encryption key (DEK) from the CMK and share the plaintext DEK with Account B via Secrets Manager cross-account sharing. Account B decrypts data using the plaintext DEK directly without accessing the CMK.
answers.C: Add Account B's specific IAM role ARN to the KMS key policy in Account A granting only kms:Decrypt. In Account B, attach an IAM policy to the processing role permitting kms:Decrypt on the specific Account A CMK ARN. To revoke, remove Account B's role from the Account A key policy.
answers.D: Create a new KMS key in Account B with the same key material imported from Account A's CMK. Grant Account B full access to their local CMK. Sync encryption using the replicated key material.

explanation: Cross-account KMS access requires both: (1) a key policy in the CMK's account explicitly granting the external account/role specific permissions (kms:Decrypt only), and (2) an IAM policy in the external account permitting the same action. This two-layer approach ensures least privilege—Account B can only decrypt, not rotate, delete, or perform other operations. Revocation is instant by removing the key policy grant. Sharing kms:* (A) grants excessive permissions. Sharing a plaintext DEK (B) exposes the raw key material and removes HSM-backed security. Importing key material to another account (D) duplicates key material, violating key management best practices.
