stem: A retailer stores millions of 2 KB product images in Amazon S3. Customers from around the world request the same popular images during flash sales, and the application team does not want to change any application logic or move the source data out of the current bucket. Which solution will provide the lowest-latency, most scalable read path?

answers.A: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket so downloads are automatically served from edge locations.
answers.B: Replicate the bucket to multiple Regions and update the application to select a Region-specific S3 endpoint for each request.
answers.C: Copy the popular objects to an Amazon EFS file system mounted in each application Region.
answers.D: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket as the origin and serve the images through CloudFront.

explanation: Amazon CloudFront is correct because it caches frequently requested S3 objects at edge locations, which reduces latency for global users and scales automatically during flash-sale traffic. S3 Transfer Acceleration improves long-distance uploads to S3, not repeated customer downloads. Multi-Region replication would increase complexity and still would not provide the same edge caching behavior without additional request-routing changes. Copying objects into Amazon EFS would add operational overhead and would not be an appropriate globally distributed read-optimization layer for this image workload.

stem: A healthcare company must migrate 280 TB of imaging data from an on-premises NAS to Amazon S3. The data center has a 500 Mbps WAN link, but after the initial migration only about 2 TB of new files arrive each week. The team wants the fastest initial transfer and a simple way to keep the S3 bucket synchronized afterward. Which approach should a solutions architect recommend?

answers.A: Copy all of the data over the WAN by using AWS DataSync and continue using the same DataSync task for weekly changes.
answers.B: Use AWS Snowball Edge devices to seed the initial data into Amazon S3, then use AWS DataSync across the WAN for the weekly incremental transfers.
answers.C: Create an AWS Storage Gateway File Gateway, copy the full data set through the gateway, and rely on its cache for the weekly changes.
answers.D: Set up an Amazon EFS file system in AWS, migrate the data to EFS first, and then replicate the data from EFS to Amazon S3 every week.

explanation: Using AWS Snowball Edge for the initial bulk transfer and AWS DataSync for ongoing deltas is correct because it avoids a very long first migration over the limited WAN link while giving the team a managed service for smaller recurring transfers afterward. Using AWS DataSync alone for all 280 TB would take much longer over 500 Mbps. AWS Storage Gateway File Gateway is designed for hybrid file access and caching, not for the fastest one-time bulk transfer of this size. Migrating to Amazon EFS first would add an unnecessary storage layer and extra copying before the data finally reaches Amazon S3.

stem: A manufacturing company runs VMware on premises and wants to expose iSCSI block volumes to existing virtual machines. explanation: Volume Gateway in cached mode is correct because it presents iSCSI block storage to the VMware environment while keeping only frequently accessed data on premises and storing the full volume dataset durably in AWS. Volume Gateway in stored mode keeps the primary data set on local disks, which does not fit the limited-capacity requirement. File Gateway presents file shares rather than iSCSI block volumes. AWS DataSync would require the team to change the backup workflow so the software writes files rather than virtual tapes. File Gateway presents SMB or NFS file shares, not a virtual tape library interface. Creating per-Region buckets and replicating between them adds operational overhead and delay before the data reaches the primary bucket. File Gateway is useful for hybrid file access, but it does not directly solve internet upload retry semantics for large client-side file transfers. explanation: EC2 instance store is correct because the checkpoint files are temporary, performance-sensitive, and can be recreated from durable data in Amazon S3 if a node fails. Amazon EFS would add shared-file-system overhead for data that does not need to be persistent. Gp3 volumes would provide persistence the team does not need and would increase cost. Writing checkpoints directly to Amazon S3 would sacrifice the low-latency local write path the simulation requires.
